THE DESIGN.  `core_euclid_strict` is a combinational circuit with 22 input pins
u0..u10 and v0..v10, each a 3-bit two's-complement integer (so every coordinate
is in -4..3), one `valid` input, and three output pins: certified, refuted,
refused.  With valid = 1 exactly one output is high.  It decides whether two
integer vectors in Z^11 meet at an angle of at least 60 degrees:

    p = u.v   s = u.u   t = v.v            (three dot-product adder trees)
    in_box    = every coordinate satisfies -3 <= x <= 3   (the code point -4 is
                outside the declared box, and an out-of-box pair is REFUSED)
    certified = in_box and ( p <= 0  or  4*p^2 <= s*t )
    refuted   = in_box and   p > 0  and  4*p^2 >  s*t
    refused   = not in_box   (the datapath itself is complete: with 8-bit
                operands no in-box pair is ever refused for width)

Inside: each of the 22 products x*y is a 3x3-bit signed multiplier; the three
sums run through chains of adders (p is 10 bits signed, s and t are 9 bits
unsigned).  If p <= 0 the trivial branch certifies without the comparator.
Otherwise la = lb = 2p (8-bit unsigned, so 4p^2 = la*lb) and ra = s, rb = t go
to a comparator submodule `cmp` that forms lp = la*lb and rp = ra*rb (16 bits
each) and fires le = (lp <= rp) or gt = (lp > rp).  A `wide` flag fires if any
comparator operand is >= 256; no in-box pair reaches it.

Fourteen million certified pair verdicts from finished mathematics were run
against this netlist and could not see some of its mutants: every vector in
that corpus has u.u = v.v = 4, so any defect that only shows when the norms
differ, or when a coordinate is out of the box, or when |u.v| is near its
maximum of 99, is invisible to it.

THE TASK.  One mutation may have been applied to this netlist -- a single bit of a
single cell's port bent -- or none at all.  Name one to eight input pairs (u, v) on
which the mutant's three output pins differ from the original's, or answer
EQUIVALENT if no input pair with valid = 1 can tell them apart, or UNDECIDED.

THE PROFILE.  The mutation's location is not given.  Four testbenches were run
against this mutant; each is 4000 pairs:

  certified corpus   4000 pairs from the 14.95M-pair certified corpus; every vector has u.u = v.v = 4 and u.v is in -4..4 -> KILLED
  near-boundary mint 4000 pairs with D = 4(u.v)^2 - (u.u)(v.v) in {-2,-1,0,1,2}; the norms differ                        -> KILLED
  out-of-box         4000 pairs with one to three coordinates equal to -4, the excluded code point                       -> SURVIVED
  aligned            4000 pairs with |u.v| at least 60 of its maximum 99 (near-parallel or near-antiparallel)            -> KILLED

ANSWER with JSON, and nothing after it:

  {"verdict": "EQUIVALENT", "where": "why no pair can tell them apart"}
  {"verdict": "UNDECIDED"}
Coordinates must be integers in -4..3 (the pins are 3-bit).  At most 8 pairs.
A KILL scores only if at least one pair actually flips a pin in simulation.  Claiming
KILL on a design that is provably unchanged, or EQUIVALENT on one that a pair can

content.text:
Looking at this problem, I need to reason about where a single-bit mutation could hide from all four adversarially-designed testbenches simultaneously.

**Coverage analysis of the four testbenches:**

- **certified corpus**: exercises typical in-box behavior with u.v small, norms equal (4).
- **near-boundary mint** (D ∈ {-2..2}): specifically stresses the comparator's boundary logic (le/gt decision) across *varying* norms — this would catch any off-by-one error in the `lp <= rp` vs `lp > rp` decision, or any adder-tree carry bug near the tie point.
- **aligned** (|u.v| ≥ 60): stresses the *upper* range of p, hence of la=lb=2p and of the 16-bit product lp=la·lb — this would catch any high-order-bit fault in the doubling, squaring, or comparator multiplier that only shows up for large operands.
- **out-of-box**: stresses the in_box detection logic across coordinate positions with the -4 code point, forcing refused.

Between them, these four suites cover: typical values, boundary-tie values, extreme-magnitude values, and the illegal-code-point path. That leaves essentially no legal (in_box) input region unexercised for the core datapath (adders, multipliers, comparator).

**The one genuinely dead region:** the problem statement itself establishes that for any pair with all coordinates in the *declared* box (-3..3), s,t ≤ 11·9 = 99, so la=lb=2p ≤ 198 < 256, and rp = s·t ≤ 9801 < 65536 — the `wide` flag can **never** fire for an in-box pair. And for out-of-box pairs, the output is forced to `refused` regardless of what `p, s, t, wide` compute, since `refused = not in_box` overrides everything downstream. So the value of `wide` (and any purely-single-bit fault confined to its computation or to logic gated exclusively by it) cannot influence `certified`, `refuted`, or `refused` for *any* input with valid=1 — reachable or not.

THE DESIGN.  `core_euclid_strict` is a combinational circuit with 22 input pins
u0..u10 and v0..v10, each a 3-bit two's-complement integer (so every coordinate
is in -4..3), one `valid` input, and three output pins: certified, refuted,
refused.  With valid = 1 exactly one output is high.  It decides whether two
integer vectors in Z^11 meet at an angle of at least 60 degrees:

    p = u.v   s = u.u   t = v.v            (three dot-product adder trees)
    in_box    = every coordinate satisfies -3 <= x <= 3   (the code point -4 is
                outside the declared box, and an out-of-box pair is REFUSED)
    certified = in_box and ( p <= 0  or  4*p^2 <= s*t )
    refuted   = in_box and   p > 0  and  4*p^2 >  s*t
    refused   = not in_box   (the datapath itself is complete: with 8-bit
                operands no in-box pair is ever refused for width)

Inside: each of the 22 products x*y is a 3x3-bit signed multiplier; the three
sums run through chains of adders (p is 10 bits signed, s and t are 9 bits
unsigned).  If p <= 0 the trivial branch certifies without the comparator.
Otherwise la = lb = 2p (8-bit unsigned, so 4p^2 = la*lb) and ra = s, rb = t go
to a comparator submodule `cmp` that forms lp = la*lb and rp = ra*rb (16 bits
each) and fires le = (lp <= rp) or gt = (lp > rp).  A `wide` flag fires if any
comparator operand is >= 256; no in-box pair reaches it.
